71.title: Two sets of cousins
71.hook: the Pandavas and Kauravas; one palace, two futures
71.howItsDone: Hindus know the Mahabharata through family retellings, comic books, television serials and temple recitations; tradition names the sage Vyasa as its author and Ganesha as the scribe who wrote it down.

segments.voice: Last time: After, the sandals, the coronation, and Hanuman staying as long as the story is told. Your line was the story stays. Did you tell someone a piece of it? Day seventy-one.

Every family has the cousins. You grew up together. Same holidays, same grandparents' house, same photos. And somewhere along the way, it went wrong between two sides of the family, and now there's a wedding where people sit at opposite ends of the room. The Ramayana was about one family and one enemy outside it. The other great epic, the Mahabharata, is about a family where the enemy is inside. Remember Ganesha breaking his tusk to keep writing? This is the book he was writing. This week, just the cliffhangers. The full reading comes later on the path.
screen: `EVERY FAMILY HAS THE COUSINS.` → `THE ENEMY IS INSIDE.` → `THE BOOK GANESHA WROTE DOWN.`

segments.voice: Two brothers. The elder, Dhritarashtra, was born blind, and so, by the rules of the time, he was passed over for the throne. The younger, Pandu, became king. Pandu has five sons: the Pandavas. Yudhishthira, the eldest, so honest it becomes a problem. Bhima, huge and hungry and strong. Arjuna, the archer. And the twins, Nakula and Sahadeva. Dhritarashtra and his wife Gandhari, who bound her own eyes with a cloth for life so she'd never see more than her husband, have a hundred sons: the Kauravas. The eldest is Duryodhana. Then Pandu dies young, and his five boys come to live in the palace at Hastinapura with their hundred cousins. One house. They train together under the same teachers. They eat at the same tables. And it goes bad early. Bhima, in play, keeps pinning the cousins, dunking them in rivers, shaking them out of trees. Duryodhana grows a jealousy that becomes hatred. He poisons Bhima and throws him into a river; Bhima survives. Later he has a house built for the Pandavas out of lacquer and wax, and sets it on fire; they escape through a tunnel. Here's the question at the heart of it. Whose throne is it? Duryodhana is the son of the elder brother, the one who sits on the throne now. Yudhishthira is the eldest son of the king who reigned. Both have a case. Neither lets go. The poem itself claims that whatever is here may be found elsewhere, and what isn't here is found nowhere. It starts with two sets of cousins and one house.
screen: `THE BLIND ELDER, THE YOUNGER KING.` · `FIVE PANDAVAS, A HUNDRED KAURAVAS.` · `POISON, AND A HOUSE OF WAX.` · `WHOSE THRONE IS IT?`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your breath slow. Think of a split in your own family, or a family you know well. Two sides that used to share a table. Don't pick a winner. Picture both sides at their best: the cousin who made you laugh as a kid, the aunt who drove everyone home. Notice what it costs everyone that the house is split. Then, if it feels right, think of one small thing that might someday let two people sit at the same table again. The bell holds the time.
Two sets of cousins. Five Pandavas and a hundred Kauravas, growing up under one roof with one throne between them.
Your line: one house. Today, send a small message to a relative on the other side of some family split. Just hello. Day seventy-one.

72.title: The dice
72.hook: Yudhishthira gambles a kingdom, then his brothers, then his wife
72.howItsDone: The dice game in the Sabha Parva is one of the best-known scenes of the Mahabharata, retold in homes, classical dance and theater; many Hindus point to it as the moment that made the great war inevitable.

segments.voice: Yesterday: two sets of cousins, five and a hundred, one palace and one throne. Your line was one house. Did you say hello across a split? Day seventy-two.

You've seen it, or felt it. Just one more hand. One more spin. One more episode, one more scroll, one more bet to win back what you lost on the last one. The Pandavas have done well. They've built a shining city of their own, Indraprastha, with a hall so magical that when Duryodhana visits, he mistakes a floor for a pool and a pool for a floor, and falls in, and people laugh. He goes home burning. His uncle Shakuni has an idea. Yudhishthira, the eldest Pandava, can't refuse a challenge. And Shakuni can't lose at dice.
screen: `JUST ONE MORE.` → `DURYODHANA FALLS IN THE POOL.` → `SHAKUNI CAN'T LOSE AT DICE.`

segments.voice: The invitation comes: a friendly game in the great hall at Hastinapura. Yudhishthira knows it's a trap. He says so. And he goes anyway, because a king of his kind doesn't refuse a challenge. The game begins. Shakuni throws for Duryodhana, and in the popular telling his dice are loaded; the text simply says he's a master of deceit at the game. Yudhishthira stakes a jewel and loses. Gold. Loses. A thousand chariots. His army. His treasury. His whole kingdom. Each time, he's sure the next throw will turn it. Then Shakuni says: what else do you have? And Yudhishthira stakes his brothers. The twins first. Then Arjuna. Then Bhima. He loses every one. Then he stakes himself. And loses. The hall is silent. And Shakuni says: there's one stake you haven't played. Your wife. And Yudhishthira, the man known for never lying, the son of dharma himself, stakes Draupadi. And the dice fall. Vidura, the king's wise half-brother, has begged them all to stop the game, and no one listens. The other elders in the hall, the grandfather Bhishma, the teacher Drona, the blind king, let it go on. What does the story know? Yudhishthira isn't a fool. He's the wisest of the brothers. And that's the frightening part. The dice didn't ruin him in one throw. They ruined him one reasonable-looking bet at a time, each one trying to fix the last. The hand keeps reaching, and at some point nobody, not even him, stops it. Tomorrow we'll see what happened to Draupadi in that hall. Today, just watch the hand.
screen: `HE KNOWS IT'S A TRAP. HE GOES.` · `JEWELS, ARMY, KINGDOM, GONE.` · `HIS BROTHERS. HIMSELF. HIS WIFE.` · `NOBODY STOPS THE HAND.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your hands rest in your lap. Feel them there, still. Now think of a losing streak you kept betting on. Maybe not money. An argument you kept doubling down on. A relationship you kept pouring into. A habit you kept telling yourself you'd fix tomorrow. Notice the moment, each time, when the hand reached for the next throw. Then look at your hands now, resting. Still. You can stop them. That's all. The bell holds the time.
The dice. A rigged game, a wise man who couldn't stop, and a kingdom, four brothers and a wife lost one throw at a time.
Your line: stop the hand. Today, when you catch yourself reaching for one more, of anything, put your hand down for one breath first. Day seventy-two.

73.title: Draupadi's sari
73.howItsDone: Draupadi's disrobing and the unending cloth are among the most retold Mahabharata scenes, in dance, theater and devotional song; many devotees see in it Krishna's protection of those who call on him, and in parts of south India Draupadi herself is worshiped as a goddess.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the dice, and a wise man who staked everything, one throw at a time. Your line was stop the hand. Did you put your hand down once? Day seventy-three.

Yesterday ended with the dice falling, and a woman lost in a game she wasn't even playing. Draupadi isn't in the hall. She's in the women's rooms. A servant comes to tell her she now belongs to the Kauravas and must come. And Draupadi, instead of coming, sends back a question. It's one of the sharpest questions anyone asks in the entire Mahabharata, and nobody in that hall, not the kings, not the elders, can answer it. This is a hard scene. It's about a woman humiliated in public. We'll tell it carefully.
screen: `LOST IN A GAME SHE WASN'T PLAYING.` → `SHE SENDS BACK A QUESTION.` → `A HARD SCENE, TOLD CAREFULLY.`

segments.voice: Her question is this: when Yudhishthira staked me, had he already lost himself? Because if he had, he was a slave. And what right does a slave have to stake anyone? Duryodhana doesn't answer. He sends his brother Dushasana, who drags her into the hall by her hair. Standing before the whole court, Draupadi asks again, to everyone. The grandfather Bhishma, the wisest man in the room, says the ways of dharma are subtle, and he can't say. Only one of the hundred Kaurava brothers, the young Vikarna, stands up and says she's right, and he's shouted down. Then comes the worst moment. Dushasana is ordered to strip her, in front of everyone. He grabs the end of her garment and pulls. And pulls. And the cloth keeps coming. Yard after yard after yard, a mountain of cloth piling up on the floor, until Dushasana collapses, exhausted, and Draupadi is still standing, still covered. In the version most people know, she has called on Krishna, and he answers her with cloth that never ends. In the oldest manuscripts that scholars have pieced together, the miracle is told more briefly, but the cloth still doesn't end. Either way, the one who was supposed to be shamed is the one left standing. And the hall knows it. Bhima swears a terrible vow of revenge. Omens howl. The blind king, frightened, finally offers Draupadi wishes, and she uses them to free her husbands. Her question was never answered. Her dignity was never removed. Unending.
screen: `HAD HE ALREADY LOST HIMSELF?` · `THE ELDERS CAN'T ANSWER.` · `THE CLOTH KEEPS COMING.` · `SHE'S THE ONE LEFT STANDING.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your spine be straight, the way Draupadi stood. Think of a time someone tried to shame you: a teacher, a boss, a relative, a crowd online. Remember how it felt. Now notice something: you're still here. Whatever they took, they didn't get all of you. Let that be true for a minute. Then think of someone else who's being shamed right now, in your world or in the news, and picture them covered, protected, still standing. If you pray, you can hold them there. The bell holds the time.
Draupadi's sari. The cloth that wouldn't end, and a question the whole court couldn't answer.
Your line: unending. Today, if you see someone being shamed, even in a small way, be the Vikarna: the one who stands up and says it's wrong. Day seventy-three.

74.title: Thirteen years
74.hook: exile, disguise, the year in hiding
74.howItsDone: The Yaksha's questions to Yudhishthira are often retold and taught as a dialogue on dharma, and the Virata Parva, the book of the year in hiding, is traditionally recited in some regions to pray for rain.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Draupadi's sari, the cloth that wouldn't end and the question nobody answered. Your line was unending. Did you notice anyone being shamed? Day seventy-four.

You'd think, after all that, the Pandavas would never touch dice again. They're freed by Draupadi's wishes, and they head home. And they're called back. One more game. One throw. The loser goes into the forest for twelve years, and then must spend a thirteenth year in hiding, somewhere in the world, undiscovered. If anyone recognizes them in that year, they start all over again. Yudhishthira plays. Yudhishthira loses. And five royal brothers, and a queen, walk into the forest with nothing.
screen: `CALLED BACK FOR ONE MORE THROW.` → `TWELVE YEARS IN THE FOREST.` → `ONE MORE YEAR, UNSEEN.`

segments.voice: The twelve forest years fill a huge part of the Mahabharata: sages, pilgrimages, stories inside stories. Near the end of them, the brothers, desperately thirsty, find a lake guarded by a spirit, a yaksha, who says: answer my questions before you drink. Four brothers drink anyway and fall dead. Yudhishthira stops and answers. The most famous question: what is the greatest wonder in the world? And his answer, roughly: that every day people die all around us, and the rest of us live as if we never will. He answers well enough that his brothers are given back their lives. Then the thirteenth year. They go to the court of a king called Virata and hide in plain sight, each one disguised as the last thing you'd expect. Yudhishthira, the man who lost everything at dice, becomes the king's dice companion. Bhima, the strongest man alive, becomes a cook. Arjuna, the great archer, lives as a dance teacher named Brihannala, in women's clothes, because of an old curse that now turns out to be a gift. The twins look after horses and cattle. And Draupadi, the queen, becomes a maid to the queen. It isn't safe. A powerful general of the court harasses Draupadi, and Bhima kills him in secret. But the year runs out, and they're not caught. Look at the disguises again: each of them hides inside a smaller version of their own life. Sometimes the only way through is to disappear for a while: to become smaller, quieter, someone else, and wait. The year of hiding isn't the end of who they are. It's a year of carrying who they are, secretly.
screen: `THE YAKSHA'S QUESTIONS AT THE LAKE.` · `THE GREATEST WONDER.` · `HIDING IN PLAIN SIGHT.` · `A YEAR OF CARRYING WHO THEY ARE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your breathing slow. Think of a season when you had to hide. Maybe you hid what you believed, or who you loved, or how bad things were. Maybe you had to take a job far beneath what you could do, or keep quiet to stay safe. Remember what you carried in secret the whole time. Don't judge that season. It got you through. Then think: is someone around you hiding right now? What might they be carrying that nobody sees? The bell holds the time.
Thirteen years. Twelve in the forest, and one in hiding, in plain sight, at a king's court.
Your line: the year of hiding. Today, be gentle with someone who seems smaller or quieter than they are. You don't know what they're carrying. Day seventy-four.

75.title: Krishna the negotiator
75.hook: five villages; Duryodhana refuses a needle's point of land
75.howItsDone: Krishna's peace mission, the Udyoga Parva's embassy, is told in Mahabharata recitations and dance dramas such as Kathakali, and 'not a needle's point of land' is a saying many Indians use for stubborn refusal.

segments.voice: Yesterday: thirteen years, twelve in the forest and one hiding in plain sight. Your line was the year of hiding. Were you gentle with someone quiet? Day seventy-five.

Have you ever tried to make peace between two people who both think they're right? You go back and forth. You shrink the ask. You offer the smallest possible thing that might let everyone save face. The thirteen years are over. The Pandavas kept every term of the bet. Now they want their kingdom back. Duryodhana says no. Both sides start gathering armies from every kingdom in the land. And one person tries, one last time, to stop the war. Krishna. Cousin to the Pandavas, friend to Arjuna, and, as many Hindus believe, God himself on earth. He goes to Hastinapura, alone, as an envoy of peace.
screen: `MAKING PEACE BETWEEN TWO SIDES.` → `THE TERMS WERE KEPT.` → `KRISHNA GOES, ALONE, FOR PEACE.`

segments.voice: Duryodhana prepares a feast to win him over. Krishna refuses it and goes instead to eat at the house of Vidura, the king's wise and humble half-brother. A small, telling choice. Then he stands in the great hall, in front of the blind king, the elders, and Duryodhana, and speaks for peace. Give the Pandavas their half of the kingdom, he says. And when that's refused, he makes the smallest ask the story knows. Give them five villages. Just five. One for each brother. They'll accept that and there will be no war. Think about that offer. Kings who once ruled a shining city, after thirteen years of exile, asking for five villages. And Duryodhana's answer has become a proverb across India. In the story, he says he won't give them even as much land as can be pierced by the point of a needle. Not without a war. His own parents beg him. The elders beg him. He walks out of the hall. He even plots to seize Krishna. And in the tradition, Krishna reveals himself in that moment, showing the court a vast, blazing form filled with gods and worlds, so bright that only a few can look. Then he leaves. The war is coming. Here's what the story knows. Wars rarely start over something big. They start when someone refuses something small. Five villages would have saved millions, in the story's numbers. A needle's point of land was too much to give. Most family fights, most feuds, have a five-villages moment: a small, fair ask that one side just won't grant.
screen: `THE FEAST REFUSED; VIDURA'S TABLE.` · `HALF THE KINGDOM. THEN FIVE VILLAGES.` · `NOT A NEEDLE'S POINT OF LAND.` · `WARS START WHEN THE SMALL ASK IS REFUSED.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe slowly. Think of a conflict in your life, big or small, that's stuck. Now look for its five villages: the smallest fair thing that could let it move. An apology. One phone call. Giving back one thing. Letting someone else be right about one point. Maybe it's something you could offer. Maybe it's something you've been refusing. Don't decide anything yet. Just find the five villages, and hold them. The bell holds the time.
Krishna the negotiator. The envoy who asked for half a kingdom, then five villages, and got not even a needle's point.
Your line: five villages. Today, in one argument, make the smallest fair offer you can, or accept one someone makes to you. Day seventy-five.

76.title: The eve
76.hook: both armies camped; the conch shells; Arjuna's hands shake
76.howItsDone: The Bhagavad Gita, which opens on this scene, is recited daily by many Hindus, often chapter by chapter; the conch shell is still blown in temples and homes at the start of worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Krishna the negotiator, five villages, and not even a needle's point of land. Your line was five villages. Did you make one small, fair offer? Day seventy-six.

The night before something big. The exam, the surgery, the wedding, the first day. You lie awake and the whole thing plays in your head. A wide plain in north India, called Kurukshetra. Two armies camped on it, bigger than any the world had seen, the story says: kings from every corner of the land, elephants, chariots, horses, foot soldiers stretching to the horizon. Tomorrow cousins will fight cousins. Far away in the palace, the blind king Dhritarashtra can't see any of it. So he asks his charioteer, Sanjaya, who has been given the gift of seeing the battlefield from afar, to tell him what's happening.
screen: `THE NIGHT BEFORE.` → `KURUKSHETRA: TWO ARMIES.` → `THE BLIND KING ASKS.`

segments.voice: His question is the very first line of the Bhagavad Gita. In Sanskrit it begins: dharmakshetre kurukshetre samaveta yuyutsavah. On the field of dharma, the field of the Kurus, gathered, eager to fight: what did my sons and the sons of Pandu do? Notice what he calls it. Not just a battlefield. A field of dharma. The Gita, which we'll read line by line in a later camp, begins here. Sanjaya tells him. The grandfather Bhishma, commander of the Kaurava army, blows his conch shell, a sound like a lion's roar. Then the other side answers. Krishna, who has agreed to drive Arjuna's chariot, lifts his conch, named Panchajanya. Arjuna blows his, named Devadatta, the god-given. Bhima blows a huge one. Conch after conch, until the sound shakes the sky and the earth. Then Arjuna says to Krishna: drive my chariot out between the two armies. I want to see who I'm fighting. So Krishna drives into the empty space in the middle. And Arjuna looks. And there, on the other side, he sees his grandfather Bhishma, who raised him. His teacher Drona, who taught him to shoot. His uncles, his cousins, his friends' sons. And the greatest archer in the world starts to shake. In the Gita's words, as closely as we can put them: his limbs give way, his mouth goes dry, his skin burns, his hair stands on end, and his great bow slips from his hand. He can't fight. He sits down in the chariot. And that's where Camp 2 leaves him, on the eve.
screen: `ON THE FIELD OF DHARMA.` · `THE CONCH SHELLS ANSWER EACH OTHER.` · `DRIVE ME BETWEEN THE ARMIES.` · `THE BOW SLIPS FROM HIS HAND.`

segments.voice: Sit, and notice your hands. Are they calm or restless? Think of something you're on the eve of: a conversation, a decision, a change, a hard day tomorrow. Let yourself feel what Arjuna feels, if it's there. The dry mouth, the heavy limbs. Don't push it away. It's allowed. Arjuna's fear is where the Gita begins, not where it ends. Now just breathe with it. Slow in, slower out. Let your hands rest open. You don't have to be ready yet. It's only the night before. The bell holds the time.
The eve. Two armies on the field of dharma, the conches sounding, and the greatest archer in the world with shaking hands.
Your line: the night before. Tonight, if something big is coming, let yourself be scared of it for one honest minute, then rest. Day seventy-six.

77.title: Camp 2 close
77.hook: Krishna takes the reins; the stories you now carry
77.tomorrow: Janmashtami: the night Krishna was born
77.howItsDone: Many Hindus picture Krishna as Parthasarathi, Arjuna's charioteer, and the image of Krishna holding the reins while Arjuna listens is one of the most common in Hindu homes, temples and on the covers of the Bhagavad Gita.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the eve, the conches, and Arjuna's bow slipping from his hand. Your line was the night before. Did you let yourself feel it, then rest? Day seventy-seven.

Before the war, before the conches, there's a scene the Mahabharata tells almost like a joke. Arjuna and Duryodhana both go to Krishna to ask for his help in the coming war. Krishna is asleep. Duryodhana arrives first and sits proudly by his head. Arjuna comes in and sits quietly at his feet. Krishna wakes, and the first person he sees is Arjuna. So Krishna makes an offer. On one side, my whole army, a vast force of warriors. On the other side, me. Alone. And I won't lift a weapon in the war. Choose.
screen: `TWO COUSINS AT KRISHNA'S BED.` → `ONE AT HIS HEAD, ONE AT HIS FEET.` → `MY ARMY, OR ME, UNARMED.`

segments.voice: Arjuna, asked first, chooses Krishna. No army. Just him. Duryodhana can hardly believe his luck: he gets the army. And then Arjuna asks Krishna to do one thing: drive my chariot. So God, as many Hindus understand Krishna, becomes a driver. In Sanskrit, a sarathi, the one who holds the reins. Krishna is still called Parthasarathi, the charioteer of Arjuna, and there are temples to him by that name. That's where Camp 2 ends: a frightened man sitting in a chariot, and the one holding the reins about to speak. Now look back at what you're carrying. Fifty-five stories. A boy made from earth guarding a door, and an elephant head. The broken tusk that finished the Mahabharata. A mouse carrying a god: vahana. A sweet that comes back to you: prasad. A baby grabbing at the sun, a leap across the sea, a burning tail, a mountain carried whole: sankat mochan. A king with no sons, a bow, fourteen years, sandals on a throne, the forest years: vanaprastha. A golden deer. Lakshmana rekha. An old bird who tried. Shabari's berries. A squirrel on Rama Setu. A foot nobody could lift. Ten heads, a hymn to the sun, a queen's grief. Agni pariksha, the scene we didn't tidy up. Diwali, the lamps. And then cousins, dice, a cloth that wouldn't end, five villages, and the eve. Here's the point of all of it. When someone mentions Hanuman now, or Draupadi, or Bharata's sandals, you won't nod politely. You'll know. You know these people now. Next, the practices, the things these stories were pointing at all along. And when a festival's date arrives, its story comes first. Tomorrow: the night Krishna was born.
screen: `ARJUNA CHOOSES KRISHNA, UNARMED.` · `SARATHI: THE ONE WHO HOLDS THE REINS.` · `FIFTY-FIVE STORIES YOU CARRY.` · `YOU KNOW THESE PEOPLE NOW.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your breath settle. Picture a chariot, and someone steady holding the reins. Now let the stories walk past, one at a time, like faces at a crowded station. Ganesha. Hanuman. Sita. Lakshmana. Jatayu. Shabari. Vibhishana. Mandodari. Draupadi. Arjuna. Don't try to remember everything. Just notice which face stops and looks at you. That's the one you're carrying out of this camp. Let it ride with you for the rest of the sit. The bell holds the time.
The driver. Sarathi, the one who holds the reins: Krishna, choosing to drive Arjuna's chariot instead of fighting.
Your line: you know these people now. Today, tell someone about the one character who stopped and looked at you. Camp 2 is done. Day seventy-seven.

original.note: Sanskrit: sarathi, a charioteer. Krishna is called Parthasarathi, Arjuna's charioteer.

trapdoor: what you thought: Krishna was Arjuna's driver, a small job.
what it means: offered a whole army, Arjuna chose Krishna alone, and asked him to hold the reins.
what a scholar hears: sarathi, the charioteer; the Gita is spoken from driver to warrior. Parthasarathi, 'charioteer of Partha' (Arjuna), names temples in the south.
